Collectively, this strategy demonstrates robust anti-pruritic efficacy, coordinated remodeling of immune and microbiota homeostasis, offering a promising platform for precision AD therapy.

title: Terminal-overhang-restricted CRISPR logic nanodevice for precision cancer therapy
abstract: The limited precision of controlled drug release remains a major challenge for precision cancer therapy. Herein, a protein and nucleic acid dual-biomarker-responsive CRISPR AND logic nanodevice, termed LogiCas, is developed by integrating APE1 and miRNA-21 as dual inputs for precise tumor therapy. Leveraging the stringent conformational matching required for Cas12a activation, LogiCas utilizes the terminal redundancy restriction of the split activator to establish a dual-lock, stepwise activation mechanism consisting of APE1-mediated pre-unlocking and miRNA-21-mediated terminal activation, enforcing tightly gated control over Cas12a trans-cleavage. The activated Cas12a further cleaves Ce6-BHQ3 to trigger Ce6-mediated photodynamic therapy (PDT), generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) that in turn drive the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic translocation of APE1, contributing to an APE1-mediated positive feedback effect. In a nude mouse model, LogiCas achieves tumor-site-specific drug release, demonstrating robust antitumor efficacy with ∼91% tumor inhibition, without obvious systemic toxicity. This work provides a new design strategy for integrating protein and nucleic acid biomarkers across molecular levels to enable CRISPR-mediated precision therapeutic activation.

title: Lung surfactants as a component of lipid nanoparticles for pulmonary mRNA delivery
abstract: Pulmonary delivery of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) remains an area of significant interest, given the broad range of genetic disorders that could be addressed through localized administration of therapeutic nucleic acids to the lung. In this study, we investigated how incorporation of the clinically used lung surfactant cocktail Poractant alfa affects the in vitro and in vivo transfection performance of mRNA-loaded LNPs. The resulting lung surfactant-enhanced LNPs (Surf-LNPs) exhibited substantial improvements in particle assembly, yielding ∼1 order of magnitude higher particle concentration at equivalent input conditions compared to conventional (Onpattro-like) LNP formulations. In vitro, Surf-LNPs demonstrated several-fold increases in mRNA transfection efficiency and protein expression while maintaining excellent cytocompatibility. These enhancements are attributed to an elevated apparent pKa and the surface-active properties of surfactant protein B (SP-B), which promote more rapid and efficient endosomal escape relative to conventional LNPs. In vivo evaluation following intranasal administration further revealed enhanced mCherry expression in the lungs of mice treated with Surf-LNPs compared to conventional LNPs. Ultimately, these findings establish lung surfactant incorporation as a simple yet powerful formulation strategy to improve pulmonary gene delivery using LNPs, with the potential to significantly advance the translation of inhaled nucleic acid therapeutics.

title: Harnessing reactive oxygen species for advanced drug delivery and therapeutics
abstract: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) have a unique position at the intersection of biology, chemistry, materials science, and medicine. They are indispensable mediators of physiological signalling, host defence, tissue remodelling, and cellular adaptation, yet their dysregulation is intimately associated with cancer, chronic inflammation, infection, metabolic disease, cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disorders, tissue injury, and ageing. This duality has made ROS both a therapeutic target and an attractive biological trigger for drug delivery. The Journal of Controlled Release Special Issue on "Harnessing Reactive Oxygen Species for Advanced Drug Delivery and Therapeutics" brings together a diverse collection of contributions that together present an important transition in the field. ROS-based delivery is moving beyond the conventional concept of a material that simply responds to an elevated oxidative environment. The contributions assembled here demonstrate that ROS can be scavenged, generated, amplified, buffered, spatially confined, chemically translated into drug release, coupled to immune modulation, integrated with metabolic sensing, and incorporated into theranostic and adaptive therapeutic systems.

title: Synthesis of cyclic oligomeric squaramides for oral protein delivery to treat inflammatory bowel disease
abstract: Cyclic squaramide oligomers are attractive supramolecular building blocks, but their use as biomolecular delivery materials remains underexplored. Here, we report the one-step preparation of a low-molecular-weight cyclic oligomeric squaramide (COS) mixture by equimolar condensation of dimethyl squarate and 2,2'-diamino-N-methyldiethylamine. Reaction-condition studies and comparative DFT-refined scan calculations indicate that linker architecture and competing hydrogen-bonding interactions influence cyclic oligomer formation. In aqueous buffer, COS forms dynamic supramolecular assemblies and associates noncovalently with copper‑zinc superoxide dismutase (SOD). The COS/SOD complexes preserved SOD activity during complexation and retained more than 70% activity after 1 h in simulated gastric fluid, whereas free SOD retained less than 20%. Their pH-dependent surface-charge change was accompanied by greater transport through mucus than a cationic formulation control. In HT-29 epithelial cells and RAW264.7 macrophages, COS/SOD increased intracellular SOD-associated fluorescence, reduced reactive oxygen species and mitochondrial dysfunction, and suppressed pro-inflammatory responses. Following oral administration in dextran sulfate sodium-induced colitis, COS/SOD improved disease activity, colon morphology, inflammatory markers, and intestinal barrier-associated outcomes. These findings position self-assembling cyclic squaramide oligomers as a supramolecular platform for oral protein formulation and delivery.

title: Barrier-reinforcing hyaluronic acid-bilirubin nanodelivery of methylprednisolone for synergistic modulation of the intestinal barrier, immune system, and gut microbiome in colitis
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is characterized by a self-reinforcing cycle of intestinal barrier dysfunction, gut microbiome dysbiosis, and aberrant mucosal immune responses. Methylprednisolone (MPS) is a potent immunosuppressant used for IBD and may beneficially modulate the gut microbiome, but its systemic adverse effects and potential impairment of epithelial repair limit its therapeutic use. To overcome these limitations, we developed MPS-loaded hyaluronic acid-bilirubin nanoparticles (MPS@HABN), an oral nanomedicine designed to protect the intestinal epithelium from MPS-associated injury while enhancing the otherwise limited immune and microbiome modulation achieved by low-dose HABN. MPS@HABN limited premature drug release, increased MPS accumulation in the inflamed colon, and reduced systemic exposure and thymic involution. It also protected intestinal epithelial cells from MPS-associated and oxidative injury. In contrast, low-dose HABN alone showed limited immune and microbiome modulation, whereas free MPS caused intestinal barrier damage and systemic toxicity such as thymic involution. In a DSS-induced colitis model, MPS@HABN improved intestinal barrier function while enhancing immune and microbiome modulation, resulting in robust therapeutic efficacy beyond that of either component alone at a low HABN dose and a clinically relevant MPS dose. These findings support combining the complementary activities of MPS and HABN to overcome corticosteroid-associated epithelial injury and the limited efficacy of low-dose HABN, thereby helping to disrupt the pathological barrier-immune-microbiome cycle in colitis.

title: The role of glycocalyx-protein corona interactions in the cell type-specific uptake of mRNA nanocarriers
abstract: Non-viral nanocarriers for oligonucleotide delivery have enormous therapeutic potential, but the factors determining cell type-specific uptake remain incompletely understood. One major cell surface component that delivery vectors encounter is the glycocalyx. While membrane glycans are established interactors for many viruses, their impact on non-viral particles has remained underexplored. Here, we show that the role of membrane glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) in mRNA delivery differs across nanocarrier categories and cell types. We employed novel glycosylation inhibitors as well as enzymatic strategies to modulate the glycocalyx, and measured their effects on mRNA delivery efficiency. Metabolic labelling enabled colocalization analysis of glycans with mRNA. Whereas lipoplexes and lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) require an intact glycocalyx for uptake by HeLa cervical cancer cells, a cationic peptide-based formulation does not. Heparan sulfate (HS) is the most important GAG for LNP uptake. Further experiments demonstrate that this interaction is mediated through HS-binding proteins of the protein corona, such as ApoE and vitronectin. HS-dependence varied across cell types: whereas HeLa and HCT116 tumor cells strongly depend on HS for LNP uptake, primary dendritic cells, normal human dermal fibroblasts, and MCF-7 breast cancer cells did not. HepG2 cells showed mild HS-dependence. Across all cell types, HS-dependence directly correlated with LNP uptake and expression, providing new mechanistic insight into why mRNA nanoparticles display cell-selective uptake.

title: Nucleus-targeted silencing of EPIC1 expression as an epigenetic strategy to modulate tumor immune microenvironment and potentiate cancer immunotherapy
abstract: Epigenetic regulation plays a pivotal role in cancer development and progression, in which long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) have emerged as one of the most important epigenetic regulators because of their ability to promote immune evasion and tumor progression. Therefore, targeted regulation of lncRNA expression could be a promising epigenetic strategy for enhanced cancer therapy, which however remains challenged due to the localization of lncRNAs in various membrane-bound organelles (e.g., nucleus and mitochondrion). We herein developed a nucleus-targeted RNA interfering (RNAi) nanoplatform for specific silencing of epigenetically induced MYC interacting lncRNA 1 (EPIC1), a nucleus-localized oncogenic lncRNA that is negatively correlated with antitumor immune response and prognosis of breast cancer (BCa) patients. Using BCa orthotopic and metastatic tumor models, we demonstrated this RNAi nanoplatform could efficiently silence EPIC1 expression in BCa cells and significantly inhibit BCa tumor growth. Mechanism study shows this EPIC1 silencing could block the function of histone methyltransferase EZH2 to catalyze the methylation of lysine 27 on histone H3 (H3K27me3) at the promoter region of its target genes, which could not only directly inhibit BCa tumor growth by up-regulating tumor suppressor genes (e.g., BAX and TP53), but also enhance the expression of immunoactive genes (e.g., MHC-I, IFN-β, CXCL9, and CXCL10) to potentiate BCa immunotherapy. Our findings indicate that EPIC1 silencing with the nucleus-targeted RNAi nanoplatform could be a promising epigenetic strategy for effective cancer therapy.

title: Metabolically engineered chimeric probiotic-cancer vesicles orchestrate anti-tumor systemic immunity
abstract: The paradigm shift toward patient-centric precision medicine has established personalized cancer vaccines (PCVs) as a key strategy for eliciting tumor-selective immunity. However, traditional cell-based PCVs face significant translational barriers, including manufacturing complexity and safety concerns. While tumor-derived extracellular vesicles (TDEVs) offer a promising cell-free alternative that recapitulates the parental tumor's antigenic landscape, their therapeutic efficacy is frequently antagonized by intrinsic immunosuppressive cargo. Here, we report ChimeraVax, a chimeric vesicular vaccine platform engineered by covalently conjugating TDEVs with Lactobacillus acidophilus-derived membrane vesicles (LAMVs) via bio-orthogonal, copper-free click chemistry. In this hybrid assembly, the TDEVs serve as a comprehensive antigen reservoir, while the LAMVs provide potent natural adjuvanticity that bypasses TDEV-mediated immunosuppression. In vitro, ChimeraVax facilitated the synchronized delivery of tumor antigens and immunostimulatory molecules to dendritic cells, significantly enhancing antigen uptake and pro-inflammatory signaling. In a murine model of aggressive triple-negative breast cancer, subcutaneous administration of ChimeraVax coordinated both innate and adaptive immune responses, yielding robust antitumor efficacy. Notably, ChimeraVax showed strict antigen dependence, selectively suppressing matched lesions with minimal effects on mismatched tumors, highlighting its specificity and translational potential as a modular personalized cancer vaccine platform.

title: Lysostaphin bioengineered cascade nanoreactor for bacterial eradication and inflammatory remodeling in MRSA pneumonia
abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) pneumonia is a life-threatening infectious disease, yet current antibiotic-centered therapies remain insufficient to achieve satisfactory therapeutic outcomes. Herein, a lysostaphin-bioengineered cascade nanoreactor, LO-PDA/Zn@CA, is developed for the integrated treatment of MRSA pneumonia. This system consists of cinnamaldehyde (CA)-loaded, Zn 2+ -chelated polydopamine nanoparticles coated with lysostaphin-engineered bacterial outer membrane vesicles. Upon reaching MRSA-infected lung lesions, CA disrupts the biofilm matrix and compromises bacterial membranes, thereby weakening extracellular protective barriers. Zn 2+ subsequently activates surface-displayed lysostaphin to specifically hydrolyze pentaglycine cross-bridges within the MRSA peptidoglycan cell wall, further breaching bacterial integrity and promoting intrabacterial penetration of CA and Zn 2+ . The released Zn 2+ induces lethal DNA damage-associated responses, collectively amplifying bactericidal efficacy through a stepwise antibacterial cascade. In parallel, the PDA/Zn nanocore scavenges excessive reactive oxygen species, suppresses glycolytic reprogramming, and downregulates H3K27ac-dependent transcription of pro-inflammatory genes, thereby attenuating macrophage M1 polarization and mitigating pulmonary inflammatory injury. In vitro and in vivo studies demonstrate that LO-PDA/Zn@CA effectively eliminates planktonic MRSA, disrupts established biofilms, and alleviates MRSA-induced pulmonary inflammation with favorable biosafety. By integrating pathogen-specific bacterial eradication with inflammation resolution in a cascade manner, this work provides a versatile nanotherapeutic strategy for the treatment of drug-resistant MRSA pneumonia.

title: Systemic tumor eradication by single-modality immunogenic neutron radiotherapy via size-controlled boron-10-enriched nanoparticles
abstract: Photon-based radiotherapy is a mainstay of cancer treatment but rarely induces systemic tumor rejection alone. Boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT) is a promising alternative consisting of neutron radiation and boron drug administration. However, systemic antitumor response by BNCT typically requires additional immunomodulator and high boron drug dosages, raising safety concerns. Herein, we develop a low-dose nanoparticle (NP)-mediated immunogenic neutron radiotherapy to eradicate tumor systemically without external immunomodulator. To realize this, we synthesize poly(glycerol)-functionalized boron-10 carbide NPs with 50 nm size ( 10 B₄C(50)-PG), which exhibit superior tumor targeting and retention properties to the other sizes we evaluated. Upon neutron irradiation, 10 B₄C(50)-PG achieves efficient tumor eradication or suppression across various murine tumor models at a lower dosage (12 mg kg -1 ) as compared with most of the boron drugs including the clinically approved boronophenylalanine (500 mg kg -1 ). Moreover, antitumor immunity is boosted after BNCT in multiple tumor models to elicit abscopal effect treating both neutron-irradiated and non-irradiated tumors, and immune-memory preventing tumor recurrence. Additionally, minimal side effects are observed in one-year safety study. Overall, our finding demonstrates 10 B₄C(50)-PG-BNCT for systemic tumor rejection, which may address the limitation of radiotherapy to elicit systemic antitumor immunity with a favorable safety profile. Moreover, this study identifies NP size as a key parameter for improving tumor delivery efficacy of boron drugs, enhancing BNCT-induced antitumor immunity.

title: Sequence-dependent self-assembly and carbon monoxide release of peptide–flavonoid conjugates for infected wound healing
abstract: Multidrug-resistant bacterial infection has become increasingly severe due to the abuse of antibiotics. Recently, carbon monoxide (CO)-based gas therapy has stood out as a novel strategy to overcome antimicrobial resistance and clear infection. However, the application is hindered by the reactive gas nature and poor precise loading. Herein, we developed a peptide-based delivery strategy by covalently binding the photo-sensitive CO donor 3-hydroxylflavone (3-HF) to the N-terminus of antimicrobial peptides (AMPs), achieving controllable and quantitative loading of CO donors. Meanwhile, by altering the amino acid sequences of AMPs, constitutionally isomeric AMP-HF conjugates underwent distinct assemble behaviors and formed different morphologies, leading to distinct light-triggered CO-releasing patterns. In vitro experiments revealed that the sequence-dependent CO-releasing behavior could enhance the antibacterial and anti-inflammatory capacity of AMP-HF conjugates to different extents. In vivo results further confirmed that AMP-HF conjugates could differentially eliminate bacteria and reconstruct the inflammatory environment at the infected site to accelerate the wound healing process.

title: Microenvironment-informed carrier-free maltol-arginine nanoparticles harness CAT2-associated arginine transport for spermatogenic disorders
abstract: Spermatogenic disorders are a major cause of male infertility, with oxidative stress-driven Leydig cell dysfunction serving as a key pathological contributor. However, effective antioxidant therapy remains limited by insufficient accumulation in injured testes and by the formulation complexity associated with conventional carrier-based delivery systems. Here, we investigated the pathological microenvironment of di(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP)-injured testes and found increased inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) expression together with upregulation of the cationic amino acid transporter 2 (CAT2) in the testicular interstitium, indicating altered arginine metabolism and transport. Based on this pathological feature, we constructed carrier-free maltol-arginine nanoparticles (MAS) through Mannich reaction-mediated covalent conjugation and non-covalent self-assembly. In this system, the arginine moiety functions as a CAT2-recognizable structural cue for lesion-oriented delivery, whereas maltol provides antioxidant activity for redox regulation. MAS preferentially accumulated in injured testes and showed enhanced uptake by Leydig cells in vitro. Mechanistically, MAS promoted Nrf2 nuclear translocation, improved redox homeostasis, and attenuated NF-κB/NLRP3/GSDMD-mediated pyroptotic signaling. In the murine injury model, MAS ameliorated testicular microenvironmental disruption, improved Leydig cell-associated endocrine function, and enhanced sperm quality. Overall, this study presents a functionally engineered, carrier-free biomaterial strategy that redirects pathology-related arginine transport remodeling into a metabolic delivery advantage, providing a viable strategy for targeted intervention in spermatogenic disorders and restoration of testicular homeostasis.

title: Self-immolative hydrogen sulfide and ciprofloxacin co-delivery nanosheets for enhanced treatment of bacterial keratitis
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA)-induced bacterial keratitis represents one of the most severe corneal infections usually accompanied by prominent inflammatory infiltration. Clinical fluoroquinolone-based therapies yield unfavorable therapeutic outcomes due to the insufficient ocular bioavailability and compromised anti-inflammatory efficacy. In the present work, we report a molecularly engineering strategy to conjugate ciprofloxacin (Cip) with a self-immolative carbonyl sulfide (COS)/hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) donating motif. The resulting prodrug (termed ASCip) could spontaneously self-assemble into nanosheets in aqueous solution, thereby improving ocular surface retention and drug bioavailability. Importantly, ASCip could be specifically activated by aminopeptidase N (APN), which is overexpressed at the inflammatory sites, enabling the controlled and simultaneous release of Cip and H 2 S, to realize antibacterial and anti-inflammatory effects. In vitro evaluations of this carrier-free nanoantibiotic revealed potent antibacterial activity against PA upon APN activation, favorable biocompatibility, and significant anti-inflammatory effects via modulating the inflammatory mediators and promoting macrophage polarization towards the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype. In a murine model of PA-infected keratitis, the nanoantibiotic efficiently eradicated pathogens, attenuated ocular inflammation, and remarkably accelerated corneal repair, providing a promising strategy to improve the efficacy of fluoroquinolone-based therapies against bacterial keratitis. More importantly, the strategy developed provides a versatile way to co-deliver COS/H 2 S with other functional motifs.

title: Combining imaging strategies with physiologically-based pharmacokinetic modeling to improve precision dosing & drug delivery in brain tumors
abstract: Small molecule targeted therapies frequently fail to control brain metastases and primary brain tumors even when systemic exposure reaches toxicity-limiting levels. Systemic exposure-response relationships are often absent, which is well documented for tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Target-site information is therefore needed, since the concentration reached in the tumor is determined not by plasma exposure, but by passive and active transport across the blood-brain barrier and by intratumoral heterogeneity. Physiologically-based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling provides the mechanistic framework to describe this. Models built solely on in vitro -to- in vivo extrapolation of permeability and transport have repeatedly required correction factors derived from rodent data, and their evaluation in humans still depends on invasive sampling or microdialysis. Microdialysis performs poorly for lipophilic, highly protein-bound drugs. We argue that quantitative imaging can supply the missing in vivo input. In a hybrid strategy, in vitro -derived transport parameters serve as the starting point, while blood-brain barrier influx and efflux are recalibrated on positron emission tomography (PET) microdose measurements in patients. This could lead to improved prediction of brain concentrations at therapeutic doses and allows simulated target-site exposure to be weighed against in vitro potency for compound and dose selection. Beyond whole-brain averages, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can provide permeability and perfusion parameters longitudinally and in larger cohorts, whereas mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) techniques can map intratumoral heterogeneity in drug distribution in the tumor microenvironment and identify potential sanctuary sites. We map each modality onto the specific PBPK parameters it can inform, and argue that imaging-informed, spatially resolved PBPK is a realistic route toward model-informed precision dosing in neuro-oncology. • PBPK (physiologically based pharmacokinetic) models can predict target-site concentrations inside the brain. • Inter- and intratumoral heterogeneity complicates brain tumor drug penetration. • IVIVE ( in vitro – in vivo extrapolation)-based brain PBPK models still need in vivo data for calibration. • Imaging techniques can capture tumor heterogeneity, sanctuary sites, and blood–brain barrier (BBB) flux. • Spatial PBPK modeling is a natural next step toward brain tumor precision dosing.

title: Focused ultrasound for reshaping the immune microenvironment in glioblastoma
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains one of the most aggressive and treatment-resistant cancers, in part due to its highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and the restricted therapeutic access imposed by the blood brain barrier (BBB). Focused ultrasound (FUS) has emerged as a promising noninvasive technology capable of transiently opening the BBB, enhancing localized therapeutic delivery, and directly modulating immune responses within the brain. Beyond its established role in drug delivery, accumulating evidence demonstrates that FUS can reshape both innate and adaptive immunity through mechanical, thermal, and cavitation-mediated bioeffects, leading to cytokine release, immune-cell recruitment, antigen presentation, and immunogenic cell death. In this review, we discuss the emerging role of FUS as an immunomodulatory platform in GBM. We first summarize the immunological consequences of different FUS modalities, including thermal ablation, histotripsy, sonodynamic therapy, and microbubble-mediated BBB opening, with emphasis on their effects on the tumor microenvironment. We then review preclinical studies combining FUS with chemotherapy, immune checkpoint blockade, CAR T-cell therapy, and nanoparticle-based therapeutics, highlighting how FUS can enhance both therapeutic delivery and antitumor immune activation. Subsequently, we examine the rapidly expanding clinical landscape of FUS in GBM, including trials focused on BBB opening, sonodynamic therapy, and sonobiopsy approaches for molecular profiling and treatment monitoring. Finally, we discuss current translational challenges, including treatment standardization, device heterogeneity, imaging requirements, and the development of next-generation ultrasound-responsive agents. Collectively, this review positions FUS not only as a delivery technology, but also as a versatile strategy for reshaping the immune microenvironment in GBM and enabling future combination immunotherapies.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-mediated co-delivery of human RB1 mRNA and triptolide for localized genetic therapy of retinoblastoma
abstract: Retinoblastoma is a rare pediatric intraocular malignancy for which intravitreal administration offers a clinically attractive route for localized therapy owing to its minimally invasive nature and direct access to intraocular tumors. However, efficient intravitreal delivery of nucleic acids remains challenging because the protein-poor vitreous microenvironment restricts nanoparticle transport and subsequent intracellular delivery. Conventional lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), which have been primarily developed for systemic administration, are therefore not necessarily suited to this unique biological environment. Here, we developed a C12-200-containing lipid nanoparticle (CLNP) engineered for efficient intravitreal gene delivery through systematic optimization of lipid composition. The optimized CLNP exhibited favorable diffusion within the vitreous, efficient intracellular mRNA delivery, and reduced dependence on extracellular protein-assisted uptake under vitreous-mimetic conditions. To demonstrate the therapeutic versatility of the platform, human RB transcriptional corepressor 1 mRNA and triptolide were co-delivered as representative gene and small-molecule therapeutics. CLNP-mediated co-delivery of hRB1 mRNA and triptolide produced greater antiproliferative activity than either monotherapy in vitro and markedly suppressed tumor progression in an orthotopic retinoblastoma model following a single intravitreal administration, with no detectable abnormalities in retinal function, structure, or apoptosis during the evaluation period. Collectively, this study establishes a vitreous-oriented lipid engineering strategy that simultaneously improves extracellular transport through the vitreous and intracellular nucleic acid delivery, providing a broadly applicable platform for localized gene delivery and combination gene-drug therapy for ocular diseases.

title: Corrigendum to ‘Glutathione-responsive copper-disulfiram nanoparticles for enhanced tumor chemotherapy’ [J. Control. Release. 341 (2022) 351–363]
An integrated prediction model using machine learning and dynamics simulation for the selection of transdermal penetration enhancers
abstract: Penetration enhancers (PEs) are widely used in transdermal drug delivery systems (TDDS) due to their cost-effectiveness and excellent biocompatibility. However, the rapid selection of PEs for TDDS is hindered by two critical challenges: first, in vitro permeation tests (IVPT) are costly and time consumption; second, the datasets for drug-PE matching are relatively limited. To address these issues, this study established a rapid screening platform for PEs in transdermal formulations using machine learning (ML) approaches based on a self-constructed database and further explored the permeation process of "drug-PE" systems via molecular dynamics simulation (MD). Systematic evaluation of five ML algorithms showed that the Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) model achieved the optimal predictive performance using 5-fold cross-validation based on random selection and unseen drug-excipient combination splitting, with R 2 values of 0.78 ± 0.03 (random split), 0.73 ± 0.01 (unseen PE split), and 0.72 ± 0.06 (unseen drug-PE combination split) on the test sets, respectively. In contrast, performance decreased substantially for the unseen-drug split (R 2 = -0.40), indicating that the model performs well primarily for interpolation within the chemical space represented in the dataset but does not reliably extrapolate to entirely unseen drugs. Feature importance analysis revealed a dose-dependent relationship between PE concentration and transdermal efficiency, while the log S of drugs exerted a non-singular effect on transdermal flux. Moreover, transdermal database analysis indicated that drugs with log P values of 2-3, when paired with PEs possessing log P values of 4-6, tended to achieve higher transdermal permeation efficiency. The accuracy of the prediction model was verified by IVPT using two model drugs, berberine and ferulic acid. Furthermore, MD simulations were employed to elucidate the penetration mechanism of the model drugs in "drug-PE" combinations at the atomic level. Finally, a rapid screening platform (https://permapp-online.streamlit.app) was developed, which enabled transdermal flux prediction through the input of molecular descriptors. This platform can provide valuable support for the future design of transdermal formulations.

title: Ischemic myocardium-targeted NAD+ nanotherapy mitigates myocardial ischemia/reperfusion injury
abstract: Myocardial ischemia-reperfusion injury remains a major cause of cardiomyocyte loss and adverse remodeling following acute myocardial infarction, yet effective therapeutic options remain limited. Although nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ) plays a central role in mitochondrial function and redox homeostasis, its therapeutic application is limited by poor membrane permeability and inefficient restoration of intracellular NAD + pools. Here, we developed a cardiac-targeted lipid-polymer hybrid nanoparticle (LN-DPC) that enables efficient intracellular delivery of NAD + to ischemic myocardium. The nanoparticale integrates boronate-guanidine-mediated NAD + encapsulation with an ischemic myocardium-homing peptide (CSTSMLKAC), achieving stable loading, controlled release, and preferential accumulation in injured cardiac tissue. In vitro, LN-DPC enhanced cellular uptake and restored intracellular NAD + levels, leading to improved mitochondrial function, reduced reactive oxygen species generation, and alleviation of calcium overload under OGD/R conditions. In vivo, the nanoparticles preferentially accumulated in the injured myocardium, attenuated early inflammation, significantly reduced infarct size, improved cardiac function, and markedly limited chronic fibrosis. Mechanistically, NAD + delivery restored SIRT3 expression, improved mitochondrial homeostasis, and suppressed HMGB1-RAGE signaling to mitigate secondary myocardial injury; pharmacological SIRT3 inhibition attenuated the protective effects of LN-DPC both in vitro and in vivo, supporting a functional contribution of SIRT3 to LN-DPC-mediated cardioprotection. Collectively, this work establishes targeted NAD + delivery as an effective strategy to restore metabolic homeostasis and protect against ischemia-reperfusion injury, and provides a nanomedicine platform for metabolic intervention in cardiovascular diseases.

title: Scalable cultured gut microbiota-derived nanovesicles for oral augmentation of checkpoint blockade therapy
abstract: Microbiota-targeted strategies, such as fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), hold promise for enhancing immunotherapy but face clinical challenges including safety risks, batch-to-batch variability, and dependence on substantial quantities of donor fecal material. To overcome these limitations, we established a standardized in vitro expansion platform for responder patient-derived gut microbiota. Through optimization of culture conditions, we achieved stable viability and retention of key immunotherapy-enhancing strains over serial passages, enabling a scalable 6.4 × 10 7 -fold expansion. Leveraging this platform, we engineered hybrid nanovesicles derived from bacterial protoplasts, followed by silica surface coating (HNVs@Silica) for oral delivery. The silica shell significantly improved nanovesicle stability under gastrointestinal conditions and conferred superior antitumor efficacy compared with uncoated counterparts. Notably, HNVs@Silica produced from the 2nd, 4th, and 6th passages retained comparable potency in augmenting anti-PD-1 (αPD-1) therapy. Mechanistically, HNVs@Silica remodeled intestinal immunity, particularly within Peyer's patches, by activating and expanding effector CD8 + T cells. This local response enhanced the priming and systemic dissemination of tumor-specific T cells, thereby improving the efficacy of αPD-1. Collectively, our findings establish a safe, scalable, and orally bioavailable alternative to FMT for enhancing cancer immunotherapy.

title: A nanocomposite hydrogel enabling spatial redox compartmentalization for endogenous Cu(I) hijacking and durable cuproptosis-mediated tumor vaccination
abstract: Cuproptosis-based in situ tumor vaccination provides a unique opportunity to transform tumor destruction into systemic antitumor immunity. However, the oxidative stress required for efficient tumor killing simultaneously disrupts immune competence through copper toxicity and immunosuppressive remodeling. Herein, we develop a spatial redox compartmentalized nanocomposite hydrogel platform to resolve this paradox by selectively amplifying intracellular cuproptosis while preserving the extracellular immune niche. Following peritumoral co-injection of gallic acid-grafted chitosan (CS-GA), dopamine-grafted oxidized hyaluronic acid (OHA-DA), and neocuproine-caffeic acid (NCP-CA) nanoparticles, the hydrogel establishes distinct redox microdomains for tumor eradication and immune protection. Specifically, NCP selectively exploits endogenous exchangeable Cu(I) pools and redirects copper toward mitochondria, where copper valence transformation and ferredoxin 1-mediated activation induce dihydrolipoamide S-acetyltransferase oligomerization, mitochondrial proteotoxic stress, and cuproptotic immunogenic cell death. Meanwhile, CA treatment was associated with increased AMPK phosphorylation and a 63.5% reduction in PD-L1 expression. Simultaneously, catechol-mediated redox cycling by CS-GA&OHA-DA continuously scavenges extracellular reactive oxygen species, alleviating oxidative immunosuppression and restoring T-cell viability to 94.4%. After 14 days of treatment, a substantial tumor regression was observed with a tumor volume reduction exceeding 64.2%. In a contralateral tumor rechallenge model, enhanced infiltration of CD8 + T-cells (40.8%) and CD8 + T EM -cells (26.4%) contributed to 75.6% inhibition of tumor recurrence and 93.3% suppression of metastasis. By exploiting endogenous copper resources rather than exogenous copper supplementation and spatially decoupling tumoricidal oxidation from immune-protective antioxidation, this hydrogel platform establishes a new approach for cuproptosis-based in situ vaccination, inducing durable antitumor immune memory and effectively preventing postoperative tumor recurrence and metastasis.

title: Phenylboronate hydrogel for administration route tailored dual-drug delivery to anterior and posterior ocular segments
abstract: Frequent multidrug eyedrop instillation for ocular perioperative prophylaxis (e.g., cataract surgery) suffers from rapid nasolacrimal clearance, limited corneal penetration, and poor access to the posterior segment. To address these limitations, we engineered an interface-adaptive phenylboronate ester hydrogel for rapid in situ gelation and the co-entrapment of two frequently instilled drugs (moxifloxacin and dexamethasone) in their free or liposomal forms at physiological pH. This platform utilizes chemical crosslinking between hyaluronic acid-conjugated 2-aminophenylboronic acid and the diols of polyvinyl alcohol (HA-2APBA@PVA), forming a dynamic hydrogel network via phenylboronate ester bonds with a thermodynamically favorable formation energy (ΔG = -10.64 kcal/mol). This unique chemistry imparts shear-thinning injectability through fine ophthalmic needles, ensures mechanical stability against blink-induced shearing, and drives robust mucoadhesion with tear film mucins such as MUC5AC for prolonged ocular retention at the injection site. Architecturally, a "liposome-in-gel" system establishes hierarchical diffusion steps that suppress the initial burst effect and extend drug release duration by >2-fold compared to the free-drug solution control. The hydrogel demonstrates excellent ophthalmic compatibility, exhibiting physiological osmolality, >80% optical transmittance, and near 100% viability in human corneal and retinal pigment epithelial cells. Safety was further validated via Draize irritation testing and preserved ocular histology across topical and periocular administration routes. Unlike the rapid washout of standard eyedrops, this hydrogel depot ensures prolonged ocular surface retention. Pharmacokinetic analysis revealed route-dependent versatility: compared to standard eyedrops, subconjunctival administration enhanced anterior segment exposure of moxifloxacin and dexamethasone by 14.9- and 8.6-fold, respectively, while sub-Tenon dosing facilitated targeted delivery to the posterior segment. This single, dynamic covalent chemistry provides a scalable, clinically compatible alternative strategy to eyedrops and advances multidrug therapies across both ocular segments.

title: Hierarchically sequential targeting nanoplatform suppresses NETosis-promoted angiogenesis for corneal neovascularization therapy
abstract: Corneal neovascularization (CorNV) lacks effective therapies due to poor drug delivery and a complex inflammatory microenvironment, necessitating a deeper understanding of the underlying pathogenic mechanisms and the development of efficient delivery systems. Here we show that neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are pathologically activated in CorNV and identify peptidyl arginine deiminase 4 (PAD4) as a key therapeutic target. To achieve coordinated inhibition of NETosis and downstream vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling, we engineer a reactive oxygen species (ROS) responsive copolymer encapsulating the PAD4 inhibitor Cl-amidine (Ca@PNH) that hierarchically targets neovascular endothelial cells and activated neutrophils via HRH and neutrophil elastase binding peptide (NEBP). Upon topical administration, Ca@PNH achieves prolonged ocular retention and lesion specific ROS triggered drug release, suppressing both NETs formation and angiogenesis. In a mouse CorNV model, this spatiotemporal strategy effectively treats neovascularization with excellent safety. Collectively, our work systematically establishes NETs as critical drivers of CorNV, identifies PAD4 as a druggable target, and offers a hierarchical delivery paradigm for inflammation driven ocular diseases.

title: Biopharmaceutics modelling of extended-release formulations with sequential TIM-1/TIM-2 biorelevant upper GI and colonic dissolution
abstract: Predicting the in vivo performance of extended-release (ER) products is difficult because drug release is excipient-controlled and may continue into the colon, a region poorly represented by conventional dissolution methods. Here, during ER formulation development, a biorelevant in vitro-in silico workflow was established to support formulation development of rocavorexant, a weakly water-soluble, high-permeability BCS II compound formulated as a HPMC-matrix ER tablet. Formulations were screened for food effect risk using the dynamic in vitro TIM-1 gastrointestinal model, before dissolution profiles measured in sequential TIM-1/TIM-2 upper-GI and colonic transit were used as dissolution input for PBBM. TIM-derived dissolution profiles were constructed from luminal samples, distinguishing apparently dissolved from dispersed drug, and from filtrate/dialysate fractions from the jejunal, ileal and colonic compartments representing dissolved drug removed from the systems. PBBM using conventional USP-I dissolution, either directly or after level A IVIVC transformation, failed to reproduce clinical pharmacokinetics, underpredicting early exposure and missing a late 20–24 h plasma plateau. Sequential TIM-1/TIM-2 input predicted clinical exposure well (predicted/observed C max 1.03; AUC 0.91–0.94), recovered the plateau and linked regional release, solubilisation, absorption and systemic pharmacokinetics.

title: Decoding extracellular vesicle–biomolecule interactions: How the biomolecular corona shapes extracellular vesicle biodistribution and clearance in vivo
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are promising endogenous nanocarriers, yet how biomolecules adsorption shapes their in vivo fate remains unclear. Here, we examine how biomolecular corona formation regulates the biodistribution, cellular recognition, and clearance of extracellular vesicles. Using EVs derived from macrophages and breast cancer cells, together with artificially prepared cell membrane-derived vesicles (CVs) generated from the corresponding parental cells as controls, we observed markedly different circulation and clearance behaviors despite their comparable physicochemical properties. Proteomic analyses revealed distinct and extensive biomolecular adsorption profiles on EVs compared with their corresponding CVs. In vivo imaging shows that EVs undergo faster systemic clearance and preferential accumulation in the liver and spleen. Cellular-level analyses identify Kupffer cells, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, splenic macrophages, and circulating innate immune cells-especially neutrophils-as key mediators of EVs clearance. In vitro studies further confirm that biomolecular corona formation enhances immune recognition and uptake, with EVs consistently showing higher phagocytosis than CVs. Notably, opsonin proteins such as complement C3 and immunoglobulins are enriched on EVs surfaces and strongly correlate with increased macrophage uptake. Overall, these results highlight biomolecular corona formation as a critical determinant of EVs biological identity and in vivo fate.

title: Mitochondria-targeted drug delivery systems for aging-related diseases: Mechanisms, strategies, and advances
abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction, characterized by increased oxidative stress, impaired energy metabolism, disrupted mitochondrial dynamics, abnormal quality control, and activation of apoptosis, represents a critical pathological basis for a wide range of aging-related diseases (ARDs), including neurodegenerative diseases, cardiovascular disorders, sarcopenia, and osteoarthritis. Mitochondria-targeted drug delivery systems increase the effective concentration of bioactive molecules within these dysfunctional organelles, offering novel strategies for the precise modulation of mitochondrial function. This review summarizes structural and functional changes in mitochondria during aging and their associations with major ARDs. We comprehensively review key advances in the design principles, mechanisms of action, and applications of passive targeting, stimuli-responsive systems, active targeting, and biomimetic drug delivery platforms. In addition, emerging interventions such as NAD + supplementation, mitochondrial gene delivery, EV-mediated mitochondrial delivery and mitochondrial transplantation are discussed. Despite the demonstrated potential of these systems to restore mitochondrial homeostasis and tissue functionality in various disease models, their clinical translation remains constrained by obstacles including unstable targeting efficacy under pathological conditions, insufficient long-term safety of materials, manufacturing complexity, and a lack of standardized evaluation criteria. Future efforts should focus on integrating disease heterogeneity, advanced materials, and multi-omics technologies to advance mitochondria-targeted therapies toward standardization, individualization, and diagnostic-therapeutic integration.

title: Annexin A5-engineered nanovaccines synchronize spatiotemporal antigen release with phagocytosis checkpoint blockade for potent in situ cancer immunotherapy
abstract: In situ generation of autologous tumor vaccines from dying tumor cells offers a promising route for personalized cancer immunotherapy, yet is often limited by phosphatidylserine (PS)-mediated immunosuppressive clearance that can restrict downstream immune activation and favor M2-like macrophage polarization. Here, we report a sequentially orchestrated nanovaccine (NT@ANX5-P) that couples photodynamic therapy (PDT)-induced immunogenic tumor-cell damage with on-demand PS masking to enhance in situ tumor vaccination. The nanovaccine consists of a photosensitizer core cloaked with genetically engineered tumor cell membranes displaying Annexin A5 (ANX5) and further shielded by a ROS-cleavable PEG layer for circulatory shielding and local light-responsive activation. Upon localized light irradiation, tumor cells undergo PDT-induced damage and apoptosis, while ROS-triggered PEG cleavage increases ANX5 accessibility for binding exposed PS, thereby attenuating PS-dependent efferocytic clearance and favoring progression toward secondary necrosis. This coordinated treatment enhanced dendritic cell maturation, remodeled tumor-associated macrophage phenotypes, and increased T-cell responses. In 4T1 tumor-bearing mice, NT@ANX5-P suppressed primary and distant tumor growth, reduced lung metastasis, and induced protection against homologous tumor rechallenge. CD8 + T-cell depletion markedly weakened bilateral tumor control, supporting an important functional contribution of CD8 + T cells. These findings provide proof-of-concept for coordinating PDT-induced antigen generation with spatially regulated modulation of PS-dependent dying-cell clearance in the 4T1 model.

title: Nanomedicine strategies for overcoming cellular and microenvironmental barriers to cuproptosis-based cancer therapy
abstract: Cuproptosis, a copper-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by mitochondrial proteotoxic stress, has emerged as a promising vulnerability for cancer therapy. However, its therapeutic translation is limited by cellular and microenvironmental barriers that restrict effective copper delivery, intracellular copper accumulation, mitochondrial engagement, and antitumor immune activation. This review summarizes the molecular basis of cuproptosis, including copper homeostasis, mitochondrial copper trafficking, lipoylated protein aggregation, and iron‑sulfur cluster disruption. We then examine how dysregulated copper transport, glutathione-mediated buffering, metabolic reprogramming, hypoxia, and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironments attenuate cuproptosis-based treatment. Focusing on these barriers, we discuss nanomedicine strategies designed to modulate copper homeostasis, deplete glutathione, reprogram tumor metabolism, alleviate hypoxia, and enhance antitumor immunity. These multifunctional platforms can enable tumor-selective copper delivery and spatiotemporally controlled activation while integrating complementary therapeutic modalities. Finally, we highlight unresolved challenges, including incomplete mechanistic understanding, tumor heterogeneity, insufficient real-time monitoring of cuproptosis, and the need to balance therapeutic efficacy with systemic copper toxicity. A systems-level integration of nanomedicine, mechanistic biology, and computational design may support the development of safer, more precise, and clinically actionable cuproptosis-based cancer therapies.

title: A dual-gated engineered bacterial platform for spatiotemporally controlled precise protein degradation
abstract: Lysosome-targeting chimeras (LYTACs) have attracted much attention due to their ability to specifically target and degrade disease-related proteins on the cell membrane. However, their clinical application is limited by poor tumor specificity, systemic off-target effects, and a lack of temporal regulation. Engineered bacteria naturally home to tumors and serve as in situ production factories, but current approaches typically lack orthogonal regulation over payload release and functional activation, leading to premature exposure and suboptimal efficacy. Here, we develop a dual-gated engineered bacterial platform (DGTPB) that decouples LYTAC delivery from functional activation. Upon tumor colonization, DGTPB constitutively produces genetically encoded LYTACs, triggers their release via L-arabinose-induced bacterial lysis, and subsequently activates targeted degradation through red-light irradiation. This dual-gating design ensures high local LYTAC concentrations while minimizing systemic exposure. We demonstrate that DGTPB-mediated degradation of EGFR and PD-L1 potently suppresses tumor growth and metastasis in both melanoma and breast cancer models. Owing to its modular architecture, DGTPB is readily reprogrammable against diverse disease-associated membrane proteins by simply exchanging targeting ligands. Collectively, DGTPB establishes a versatile, programmable, and safe framework for precision extracellular targeted protein degradation, thereby providing a new tool for engineered-bacteria-based platforms in cancer immunotherapy.

title: Mechanistic benchmarking of SNAC, DDM, and LLC reveals enhancer-dependent pathways for intestinal semaglutide delivery
abstract: The oral delivery of peptide therapeutics remains constrained by poor intestinal permeability and the challenge of enhancing epithelial transport without compromising mucosal integrity. Although sodium N-(8-[2-hydroxybenzoyl]amino) caprylate (SNAC) enables gastric absorption of oral semaglutide and has also been explored for small-intestinal absorption of other peptide drugs, its suitability for enteric intestinal delivery of semaglutide remains unexplored. Here, we performed a comparative mechanistic evaluation of three permeation enhancers (SNAC, N-dodecyl-β-D-maltoside, and lauroyl-l-carnitine) for enteric delivery of semaglutide. Mechanisms were screened in epithelial monolayers and in situ intestinal absorption in rats, and the enhancers carried forward were formulated into enteric-coated capsules and evaluated in beagle dogs, with the leading candidate taken in to cynomolgus monkeys. In differentiated Caco-2 monolayers, all enhancers increased semaglutide transport but exhibited distinct transport mechanisms and barrier-response profiles. SNAC increased permeability without increasing mannitol transport or disrupting ZO-1, indicating a largely non-paracellular, cargo-dependent profile. DDM markedly increased paracellular marker transport and disrupted tight-junction organization, consistent with a primarily paracellular mode of action associated with reduced barrier recoverability. LLC showed a more favorable balance between transport enhancement and barrier recovery, while also increasing intracellular semaglutide-associated fluorescence and FD4 permeability. Rab5 immunostaining and dynasore inhibition indicated a dynamin-sensitive uptake component alongside partial tight-junction modulation. In rats, LLC produced the greatest increase in semaglutide absorption, and this effect was substantially attenuated by dynasore co-treatment. Transmission electron microscopy and tissue immunofluorescence further supported the presence of LLC-associated micelle-like structures, Rab5-related intracellular trafficking and junctional remodelling, with no overt tissue injury on local or systemic histology. For large-animal translation, citric acid and L-arginine improved semaglutide stability in intestinal fluids, and the resulting LLC-containing enteric formulation markedly increased systemic exposure in orally dosed beagle dogs and in cynomolgus monkeys following intraduodenal delivery. Collectively, these findings identify LLC as a promising permeation enhancer within the present SNAC/DDM/LLC comparison for enteric intestinal delivery of semaglutide and highlight how coordinated uptake-related and barrier-modulating mechanisms can support intestinal semaglutide absorption.

title: Engineering whole tumor cell vaccines for cancer immunotherapy: From malignant cells to therapeutic vaccines
abstract: Tumor cells are the driving force of cancer progression, yet they also constitute a rich reservoir of tumor-associated and patient-specific antigens that can be harnessed for therapeutic vaccination. Whole tumor cell vaccines (WTCVs) exploit this unique duality by converting malignant cells into immunotherapeutic agents capable of eliciting broad antitumor immunity and overcoming tumor heterogeneity. However, their clinical translation remains constrained by the need to eliminate tumorigenic potential while preserving or enhancing immunogenicity. Here, we provide a comprehensive overview of recent advances in the engineering of WTCVs from the perspectives of safety assurance and therapeutic enhancement. We summarize current strategies for controlling tumorigenicity, including physical, chemical, engineered, and viability-preserving approaches, and discuss emerging immunopotentiation strategies that enhance antigen abundance and exposure, improve antigen presentation, activate innate and adaptive immune pathways, and integrate complementary therapeutic modalities. Collectively, these advances are transforming malignant cells into multifunctional therapeutic vaccines capable of eliciting potent and durable antitumor immunity. Finally, we discuss the key challenges and future opportunities for next-generation WTCVs and highlight design principles that may accelerate their clinical translation.

title: Gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase-responsive lipid PtIV prodrug amphiphile with tumor-selective uptake for enhanced chemotherapy
abstract: The limited tumor selectivity of cisplatin contributes to off-target exposure and dose-limiting toxicity. Here, we developed an enzyme-activatable, axially functionalized Pt IV prodrug amphiphile for γ-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGT)-responsive cellular uptake and intracellular activation. The amphiphilic prodrug, consisting of a hydrophobic hexadecyl alkyl chain and a γ-glutamyl-functionalized peptide headgroup, spontaneously self-assembled into colloidally stable nanoparticles (GPt IV ). GGT-mediated cleavage of the γ-glutamyl group shifted the surface charge of GPt IV from negative to positive and enhanced cellular uptake in GGT-high tumor cells. Pharmacological inhibition of GGT attenuated GPt IV uptake in 4T1 cells, further supporting the contribution of GGT activity to cellular internalization. Following cellular uptake, GPt IV underwent reductive activation under reducing conditions and released cisplatin. GPt IV exhibited enhanced cytotoxicity toward GGT-high tumor cells and preferential tumor accumulation in 4T1 tumor-bearing mice. At the tested Pt dose, GPt IV achieved greater tumor growth inhibition and improved renal and hepatic tolerability relative to the comparator Pt formulations. These findings support GGT-responsive charge conversion as a strategy for improving the cellular delivery and therapeutic performance of self-assembling Pt IV prodrugs in GGT-high tumors.

title: Immunosuppressive termination of pro-inflammatory miRNA degradation via circular RNA nanosponge for sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy treatment
abstract: Managing inflammatory cytokine storms is prevalent in treatment of sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy (SICM), yet it remains a challenge to immunosuppression weaning. We herein propose an immunosuppressive termination of pro-inflammatory microRNA-33 (miR-33) degradation strategy for on-demand anti-inflammatory management. Inspired by circular RNA (cRNA) sponging capacity, we designed a miR-33-targeted sequence of cRNA (cRNA-33), including 11 of miR-33 binding sites and a single microRNA-223 (miR-223)-specific immunosuppression binding site. To improve drugability, cRNA-33 is compressed into reactive oxygen species (ROS)-responsive polymeric assembly, and covered by tannic acid-modified hyaluronic acid to enhance cardiac inflammatory macrophage accumulation. Triggered by intracellular ROS, cRNA-33 rapidly dissociates from assembly and binds sufficient miR-33 to alleviate inflammatory actions of NLRP3 and IL-1β induction. Macrophages are subsequently shifted from pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory phenotype, resulting in high expression of miR-223 that destabilizes cRNA-33 through the miR-223-responsive site to discontinue immune responses. The cRNA-33 treatment yields 80% decrease of inflammation efficacy, 90% cardiac function recovery and 87.5% survival rate in study mice. Collectively, this study has provided an advanced anti-inflammatory therapy for SICM, at a safe level.

title: Triple-modal visualized radiohydrogel alleviates post-embolization hypoxia via stage-type procedure in hepatocellular carcinoma
abstract: Transarterial radioembolization (TARE) holds significant potential for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), but its effectiveness is hindered by radiation resistance from the post-embolization hypoxic microenvironment and challenges in achieving stable local release of radionuclides. Herein, polydopamine (PDA)-coated MnO 2 nanoparticles (MnO 2 @PDA) with a core-shell structure were introduced as the intratumoral hydrogen peroxide nanocatalyst, and 177 Lu was anchored in catechol groups on the PDA surface, achieving the stability of radionuclides. And the radionuclide-coordinated nanocatalyst was incorporated into the poly(ethylene oxide) and poly(propylene oxide) thermosensitive hydrogel to formulate an integrated TARE agent ( 177 Lu-MnO 2 @PDA-Gel), facilitating secondary encapsulation and ensuring intratumoral retention of radionuclides without leakage. Through a three-stage lytic process, 177 Lu-MnO 2 @PDA-Gel produced oxygen by gradually consuming endogenous H 2 O 2 . This allowed for post-embolization radiosensitivity and anti-angiogenesis. Furthermore, the release of manganese ions from the embolic hydrogel can serve as an adjuvant to boost intratumoral immune infiltration and improve the efficacy of embolization and internal radiation. Notably, the superiority of SPECT/PAI/MRI triple-modal imaging via 177 Lu-MnO 2 @PDA-Gel enables real-time and dynamic visualization of TARE. Overall, the smart hydrogel demonstrates long-term oxygen generation, stable internal radiation, and tumor microenvironment remodeling, offering a sequential radiosensitization strategy to address TARE refractoriness, thereby presenting significant clinical value for locoregional therapy of HCC.

title: Ionizable lipid impact on mRNA vaccine formulation properties and immunogenicity
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted global supply chains, causing shortages of critical lipid-based raw materials for mRNA vaccine production. To enhance formulation resilience, we systematically evaluated the impact of five ionizable lipids (ILs) on lipid nanoparticle (LNP) organization, mRNA delivery and immunogenicity. The physiochemical analysis revealed the potential coexistence of liquid crystalline lamellar (L α ) and inverse hexagonal (H II ) phases, or a mixture of nucleotide-loaded and non-loaded H II phases within developed LNP formulations. Furthermore, ILs with saturated, multi-tail structures, such as Lipid-5 and SM-102, favored inverse hexagonal (H II ) internal organization and fusion intermediates, correlating with enhanced endosomal fusion and higher in vivo protein expression. In contrast, ILs such as cKK-E12, which featured dual ionization headgroups and tended to form lamellar-like structures, showed reduced encapsulation efficiency and transfection potency. The preclinical experiments demonstrated that all developed formulations induced robust binding and neutralizing antibody responses; however, antibody responses were lower in mRNA Lipid 5 LNPs and mRNA SM-102 LNPs than in other formulations. Notably, within the limited panel of ILs in this study, protein expression levels did not show a clear correlation with antibody titers, highlighting that efficient antigen expression alone is not predictive of humoral immunity. These findings underscore how IL structural features influence LNP architecture and function, informing the rational design of next-generation mRNA vaccines.

title: Reprogramming tumor-associated macrophages via ID3 mRNA delivery for enhanced immunotherapy in pancreatic cancer
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) features a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment dominated by tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), which facilitate immune evasion and compromise immunotherapeutic efficacy. The interaction between signal regulatory protein α (SIRPα) on macrophages and cluster of differentiation 47 (CD47) on tumor cells delivers a "don't-eat-me" signal that inhibits the phagocytosis of tumor cells by macrophages. Here, we present a macrophage-directed mRNA delivery strategy to reprogram TAMs in PDAC. Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) were engineered to deliver inhibitor of DNA binding 3 (ID3) mRNA, whose expression was associated with reduced SIRPα expression and pro-inflammatory macrophage reprogramming. To promote preferential uptake by TAMs, mannose-modified LNPs (MLNPs) were developed by exploiting elevated CD206 expression on these cells. In an orthotopic PDAC model, MLNP-mediated ID3 mRNA delivery enhanced macrophage phagocytosis, promoted pro-inflammatory immune remodeling, and increased intratumoral T cell and natural killer cell (NK) infiltration, accompanied by tumor-growth suppression. Furthermore, MLNP-ID3 showed enhanced combination activity with anti-PD-1 therapy. Collectively, these findings establish a macrophage-targeted mRNA strategy for transcriptional reprogramming of TAMs and present a promising immunotherapeutic framework for PDAC.

title: Sustained degradation of glucose transporter 1 by an mRNA-encoded lysosome-targeting chimera triggers metabolic collapse and pyroptosis in cancer
abstract: Cancer cells are intrinsically addicted to glucose and require glucose transporter 1 (GLUT1)-mediated glucose metabolism for their survival. Although small-molecule inhibitors of GLUT1 have exhibited suppressive effects on tumor cells, they achieve only transient functional blockade, thereby limiting therapeutic durability and permitting metabolic escape. Here, we report MetaTAC-G1, an mRNA-encoded lysosome-targeting chimera that enables rapid and sustained degradation of cell-surface GLUT1. MetaTAC-G1 comprises a bispecific binder that bridges GLUT1 to the lysosomal trafficking receptor sortilin, thereby directing constitutive lysosomal clearance of the transporter upon translation. For local intratumoral delivery, we encapsulated the MetaTAC-G1-encoding mRNA in RGD-functionalized lipid nanoparticles (RGD-LNPs), achieving efficient MetaTAC-G1 expression and sustained GLUT1 degradation. Functionally, MetaTAC-G1 induced profound metabolic collapse in SUM159PT cells, characterized by acute ATP depletion and reactive oxygen species (ROS) accumulation, culminating in GSDMD-dependent pyroptosis. Similar pyroptosis-associated morphological changes were observed across multiple additional cancer cell lines. In vivo, a single treatment course of MetaTAC-G1 markedly suppressed tumor growth and produced durable antitumor activity without apparent systemic toxicity. Our findings highlight that sustained degradation of GLUT1, rather than transient functional inhibition, is critical for triggering metabolic cell death in tumors.

title: Overcoming the cutaneous barrier: Topical delivery platforms for targeted gene-based therapeutics in psoriasis
abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic immune-mediated skin disorder characterized by persistent inflammation, epidermal hyperproliferation, and complex interactions among immune cells, keratinocytes, cytokines, and genetic factors. Although conventional topical agents, systemic small molecules, and biologics have improved disease management, their clinical utility is often limited by insufficient efficacy, adverse effects, treatment resistance, and poor patient adherence. Recent advances in molecular biology have identified numerous pathogenic genes, signaling pathways, and regulatory RNAs involved in psoriasis, providing opportunities for the development of gene-based therapeutics, including antisense oligonucleotides, plasmid DNAs, small interfering RNAs, messenger RNAs, microRNAs, aptamers, and CRISPR/Cas9 systems. These therapeutics enable precise modulation of disease-associated targets at the genomic and transcriptional levels, offering advantages over conventional pharmacological approaches. However, their topical administration is hindered by the formidable cutaneous barrier, limited skin penetration, poor cellular uptake, and susceptibility to enzymatic degradation. This review summarizes the cellular, molecular, and genetic mechanisms underlying psoriasis pathogenesis and discusses the therapeutic potential of diverse gene-based approaches. Particular emphasis is placed on topical delivery platforms designed to overcome cutaneous barriers, including permeation enhancers, nanocarrier-based systems, and physical enhancement technologies. Recent advances in the integration of these delivery strategies with gene therapeutics for targeted psoriasis treatment are highlighted. Finally, current challenges related to delivery efficiency, long-term safety, manufacturing scalability, and regulatory approval are discussed, together with future perspectives for the clinical translation of topical gene-based therapeutics toward precision psoriasis management.

title: Functional response, retinal structure and safety of subretinal gene augmentation in retinitis pigmentosa: A systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Introduction Subretinal adeno-associated virus (AAV) gene delivery is being investigated for retinitis pigmentosa (RP), yet functional efficacy, retinal structural effects, and delivery-associated safety remain uncertain. We synthesised clinical evidence across these outcomes. Methods Six databases were searched through January 2026, with an update on September 28, 2026. Random-effects meta-analyses evaluated subretinal AAV gene augmentation; mechanistically distinct therapies were synthesised narratively. Outcomes included microperimetry, best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), full-field stimulus threshold (FST), retinal thickness, and adverse events. Follow-up and sensitivity analyses explored variability. Results Thirteen reports representing 12 studies were included; eight contributed quantitative data. Microperimetry improved by 6.72 dB (95% CI 6.45-6.98; four studies; I 2 = 0%), with most observed gains within six months. Time-stratified sensitivity estimates ranged from 2.77 dB at one month to 6.79 dB at 12 months, without establishing within-patient trajectories. BCVA improved by 4.12 ETDRS letters (95% CI 3.45-4.80; four studies; I 2 = 0%), below a conventional five-letter benchmark. Exploratory meta-regression suggested greater acuity gains with follow-up (0.27 letters/month), but cluster-robust inference was nonsignificant (p = 0.10). FST did not improve in two studies. Central retinal thickness decreased by 33.7 μm from baseline (95% CI -37.3 to -30.1; three studies), without establishing treatment-attributable thinning. Ocular adverse events occurred in 29.4% (95% CI 19.1-42.5%), and serious adverse events in 19.4% (95% CI 12.8-28.2%). Small early-phase cohorts, heterogeneous comparators, and insufficient delivery-specific comparisons constrained interpretation. Conclusion Subretinal AAV augmentation showed preliminary functional signals, but clinically meaningful benefit and structural safety remain uncertain. Controlled studies should standardize endpoints and clarify vector-, dose-, and procedure-related risks.

title: Patient-specific pharmacokinetics of intratumoral cisplatin track pathologic necrosis in early-stage lung cancer
abstract: Intratumoral injection of cisplatin into lung cancer is feasible and can increase local drug exposure while reducing systemic toxicity. However, its success relies on achieving sufficient drug exposure to the tumor, which has not been quantitatively evaluated in a clinical setting. In the context of a Phase I clinical trial of intratumoral cisplatin injections into resectable lung tumors via robotic bronchoscopy (N = 6), we developed a quantitative framework to assess delivery effectiveness and long-term cisplatin exposure in tumors. Initial injectate retention was estimated using a novel image analytics pipeline based on intraoperative cone-beam computed tomography scans, by assuming that emerging high-attenuation regions are due to injectate deposition. Long-term drug exposure was estimated using a novel pharmacokinetic model tailored for intratumoral drug delivery and informed by sequential venous blood draws following the injections. The area under the platinum concentration curve in the tumor compartment at t = 3-21 h and platinum concentration in the tumor compartment (t = 3-6 h), estimated from the fitted pharmacokinetic model, showed a strong monotonic association with percentage pathological necrosis assessed post-resection by three independent, blinded pathologists (Spearman's ρ = 0.93, 95% bootstrap CI 0.67-1.00, unadjusted exact p = 0.033), which was not statistically significant when corrected for multiple comparisons (adjusted p = 0.17). No other pharmacokinetic variable correlated was significantly correlated with necrosis or other pathological response metrics prior to multiple comparison correction. This result aligns with the known time-concentration dependency of cisplatin action in tumor. Further studies will be needed to evaluate this observation for repeatability and clinical relevance. Our approach provides a framework for estimating intratumoral drug exposure in clinical settings, which may help with the interpretation of clinical trial outcomes and future evaluation of injection strategies.

title: Fluorinated polyamidoamine-mediated delivery of miRNA-23b to alleviate inflammation and bone loss in periodontitis
abstract: Periodontitis is a chronic inflammatory disease characterized by the destruction of periodontal tissues, and is driven by dysregulated immune responses and persistent inflammation. Despite traditional treatments, effective therapeutic strategies targeting the underlying mechanism are still limited. Emerging evidence suggests that miR-23b plays a regulatory role in controlling the inflammation, but its function and therapeutic potential in periodontitis remain unexplored. In this study, the miR-23b level was identified to be significantly downregulated in gingival tissues from both clinical periodontitis patients and a rat periodontitis model. To restore its function, fluorinated polyamidoamine (FP) was employed as the carrier to achieve the miR-23b delivery into inflammatory macrophages. The FP/miR-23b nanoparticles effectively suppressed the NF-κB activation by targeting TAB2, TAB3 and IKK-α, leading to the reduced levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines. In the rat periodontitis model, FP/miR-23b nanoparticles were effectively delivered to periodontal macrophages, resulting in reduced local inflammation and inflammatory cell infiltration, and alleviated alveolar bone resorption. Meanwhile, no adverse effects on body weight or major organs were observed, suggesting the favorable biocompatibility of FP/miR-23b nanoparticles. These findings suggested that FP-mediated miR-23b delivery represented a potential therapeutic approach for periodontitis through host inflammatory modulation and alveolar bone protection.

title: A Janus adhesive sealant with extreme acid-tolerance for gastric perforation repair
abstract: Although Janus adhesive sealants hold great potential for gastric perforation repair, current versions fail to achieve stable and durable sealing in highly acidic gastric fluid. Herein, we employ the homogeneous hydrophobic strategy for the first time to develop a Janus adhesive patch with extreme acid-tolerance for gastric perforation repair. The patch is fabricated by unilaterally immersing a Cu 2+ -crosslinked lipoic acid (LA) gel into a chitosan oligosaccharide (COS) solution (Cu@LA-COS). Owing to the homogeneously hydrophobic poly(LA) network that can durably repel both water molecules and hydronium ions, the Cu@LA-COS patch maintains a stable adhesive strength exceeding 42 kPa even after 14 days of immersion in highly acidic simulated gastric fluid. In addition, the Cu@LA-COS patch exhibits anti-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic activities, achieving complete gastric wound closure in Sprague-Dawley rats with gastric perforation within 14 days, with a regenerated mucosal layer thickness comparable to that of healthy stomach. This extremely acid-tolerant Janus adhesive Cu@LA-COS patch, capable of durably sealing gastric defects and preventing postoperative adhesion, is a promising sealant for gastric perforation repair.

title: Dexamethasone palmitate-loaded nanodiscs target inflamed joints and suppress rheumatoid arthritis
abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is driven by persistent joint inflammation and dysregulated adaptive immune responses, highlighting the need for drug delivery strategies that can concentrate immunomodulatory therapy at inflamed joints and disease-associated lymphatic tissues. Here, we formulated dexamethasone palmitate-loaded synthetic high-density lipoprotein nanodiscs (DXP-NDs) as a biomimetic nanodelivery platform for subcutaneous administration and inflammation-directed delivery. DXP-NDs exhibited excellent encapsulation efficiency (95.8% ± 2.4%) and maintained their ~10 nm size for 60 days during storage either at 4 °C or 37 °C. DXP-NDs downregulated MHC-II and costimulatory molecules (CD40/CD80/CD86) on bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (BMDCs) in vitro. In the absence of a strong antigenic signal, this costimulatory blockade significantly promoted regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation. In contrast, upon strong antigen exposure, DXP-NDs aborted productive T-cell activation, suppressing proliferation and locking T cells in an unactivated, anergic state. Following subcutaneous administration, DiR-labeled nanodiscs selectively accumulated in inflamed joints in both zymosan-induced arthritis and collagen-induced arthritis models, with joint fluorescence correlating strongly with clinical paw scores. In a murine model of zymosan-induced arthritis, DXP-NDs alleviated inflammatory joint swelling and reduced regional Th1 frequencies. In a murine model of collagen-induced arthritis, DXP-ND therapy arrested clinical disease progression and reduced systemic IL-1β levels, with additional evidence of immune remodeling in draining lymph nodes. T-cell analysis revealed reduced Th1 and Th17 frequencies, decreased effector memory T-cell populations, and increased regulatory T-cell frequencies after extended treatment. Overall, these studies demonstrate that DXP-NDs traffic to inflamed arthritic joints and lymphatic tissues after subcutaneous administration and promote coordinated anti-inflammatory and immunoregulatory effects that attenuate joint inflammation and limit disease progression in murine arthritis models.

title: Biodegradable radiopaque polymeric particles for computed tomography-guided intraperitoneal drug delivery
abstract: An iodinated hydrophobic oil containing the 2,3,5-triiodobenzoate moiety was encapsulated in biodegradable poly(lactic acid)-based polymer particles using a solvent emulsion-evaporation technique that provided control over particle size. The hydrophobic iodinated oil served a dual function as radiopaque contrast agent for particle quantification using dual-energy x-ray computed tomography (DECT) imaging and furthermore as solvent for the chemotherapeutic drug paclitaxel (PTX), establishing a novel theranostic system. Release kinetics of PTX was studied in fetal bovine serum over seven days demonstrating sustainable drug release over the entire period, with cumulative release mainly depending on particle diameter. Intraperitoneal administration of a therapeutic dosage of radiopaque spheres in mice provided sufficient iodine contrast to track biodistribution and clearance over 18 days. Importantly, imaging showed unexpected particle aggregation in vivo with about 50% clearance over 18 days, emphasizing the value of real-time distribution assessment as a complementary method to conventional ex-vivo histology. A proof of concept of longitudinal dual imaging using single-photon emission CT (SPECT)/DECT was demonstrated in a mouse model of colorectal cancer with intraperitoneal metastases following a single intraperitoneal dose of PTX or PTX-loaded particles. Treatment response was monitored using SPECT, while particle distribution was tracked by DECT. This theranostic approach integrates controlled intraperitoneal drug delivery with non-invasive quantitative DECT-based imaging and may improve treatment precision and therapeutic outcomes.

title: The microbiota-drug delivery nexus: from pharmacomicrobiomics to live biotherapeutic delivery
abstract: The human microbiota, being the diverse communities of bacteria, archaea, fungi, and viruses colonising the gut, skin, respiratory tract, and urogenital system is now recognised as a critical, yet frequently overlooked, determinant of pharmaceutical outcomes. The emerging field of pharmacomicrobiomics has established that microbiota compositional and functional variation profoundly influences drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and toxicity, whilst drugs reciprocally reshape microbial community structure.
