However, a fundamental dimension of this relationship has received insufficient attention: the drug delivery system itself is not a passive vehicle but an active participant in microbiota-drug interactions. The physicochemical properties of delivery vehicles, the excipients they contain, and the pharmacokinetic profiles they impose each alter the nature, site, and duration of drug-microbe contact in ways that have significant consequences for therapeutic outcomes. Conversely, the microbiota modulates the performance of drug delivery systems through degrading carriers, altering mucosal permeability, and modifying the environment in which release occurs. Beyond these bidirectional interactions, controlled release technology offers a distinct and compelling opportunity, including the deliberate exploitation of microbial metabolic activity as a trigger for site-specific drug release and the delivery of the microbiota itself. This review introduces the concept of the microbiota-drug delivery nexus, providing the first comprehensive account of the bidirectional interactions between drug delivery systems and the human microbiota, with a specific focus on how oral and non-oral delivery vehicles interact with the gut microbiota. Critical knowledge gaps are identified, which highlight emerging opportunities for microbiota-informed formulation design, and make the case that incorporating microbiota considerations into drug delivery science is no longer optional but essential for the rational development of next-generation therapeutics.

title: Reversal of tumor-immune metabolic competition via sequential energy blockade to reactivate exhausted T cells for enhanced cancer immunotherapy
abstract: The efficacy of cancer immunotherapy is usually constrained by tumor-immune metabolic competition. Metabolic blockade therapies face metabolic plasticity, whereas simultaneous drug delivery is limited by ATP-dependent drug and ion efflux. Herein, a tumor-microenvironment (TME)-activatable yolk-shell nanoreactor comprising a calcium peroxide (CP) core, a WZB117 (WZB)-loaded cavity, a hollow mesoporous Cu-3,3'-dithiobis(propionohydrazide) shell (HMCT), and a hyaluronic acid (HA) coating (CP-WZB@HMCT@HA) was developed to execute a "starve-first, strike-later" sequential energy blockade strategy. A spatiotemporal cascade mediated by CP-WZB@HMCT@HA is activated under acidic and GSH-rich TME. Initially, disulfide-bridged shell degradation releases Cu species that deplete GSH, sensitizing tumor cells to oxidative stress. Crucially, glycolysis is inhibited by the early release of the GLUT1 inhibitor WZB, which leads to rapid ATP depletion that suppresses efflux pumps and increases intracellular retention of therapeutic agents. Subsequently, calcium overload and copper-mediated ROS generation disrupt mitochondrial homeostasis. This sequential energy blockade induces tumor energy depletion, elevates extracellular glucose levels, and reduces lactate accumulation. Consequently, immunosuppressive factors (PD-L1/TGF-β1) are downregulated, which reactivates the antitumor immune capacity of exhausted T cells. In vitro and in vivo assessments demonstrate antitumor activity and acceptable biocompatibility. This strategy provides a potential approach for remodeling tumor-immune metabolic competition and improving cancer immunotherapy.

title: Rationally designed negatively charged lipid nanoparticles reduce systemic reactogenicity of mRNA vaccines while preserving immunogenicity
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines have emerged as versatile platforms for the prevention of infectious diseases and therapeutic cancer vaccination. However, strong reactogenicity remains a key challenge, with severe adverse events such as myocarditis. These concerns may limit the applications of mRNA vaccines. As lipid nanoparticles (LNP) are the primary driver of inflammation, optimizing LNP composition is a promising approach to reduce mRNA vaccine reactogenicity. However, the effects of tuning the physicochemical properties of LNP, particularly their surface charge, remain insufficiently characterized. In this study, we aimed to engineer negatively charged LNPs by incorporating anionic phospholipids and evaluate their biodistribution, immunogenicity, and adverse reactions in mice. Negatively charged LNPs significantly reduced systemic inflammatory responses and fever compared to a conventional LNP. Moreover, cardiac troponin I-a marker of myocarditis-was reduced in negatively charged LNPs. Despite reduced systemic reactogenicity, negatively charged LNPs maintained antigen-specific immunogenicity comparable to a conventional LNP. The negatively charged LNPs did not attenuate local inflammation at the injection site. This local inflammation depended on the fatty acyl chain of phospholipids in the LNP and was independent of the head group structure or negative charge. Surface charge modulation also reshaped biodistribution to distal organs, such as the spleen and liver. Correlation analysis linked reduced reactogenicity to decreased hepatic delivery of LNPs, and prior datasets supported this relationship. Taken together, our results establish phospholipid-driven surface-charge control as a promising approach to reduce systemic reactogenicity while maintaining the immunogenicity of mRNA vaccines.

title: Redox-responsive nanoparticles prevent post-ablation hepatocellular carcinoma recurrence by dual regulation of dendritic cells and tumor cells
abstract: Radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is a locoregional therapy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). However, the long-term efficacy for RFA is severely compromised by recurrence driven by an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). In this study, we identify mature regulatory dendritic cells (mregDCs) as a key immune-regulatory population closely associated with this immune evasion. Following insufficient RFA (iRFA), sublethal thermal injury induces excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) and hypoxia, which synergistically promote mregDC differentiation and upregulate PD-L1, leading to profound CD8 + T cell exhaustion. To address these challenges, we developed a redox-responsive nanoplatform for co-delivery of an ROS scavenger N-acetylcysteine (NAC) and siPD-L1. This nanoplatform effectively mitigates hypoxia and oxidative stress within the TME while reprogramming mregDCs toward an immunostimulatory phenotype via PD-L1 silencing. In both subcutaneous and orthotopic iRFA-HCC models, treatment with NPs(siPD-L1/NAC) potently activates CD8 + T cells, suppresses tumor growth, and exhibits a favorable safety profile. Our findings uncover an mregDC-mediated immune evasion mechanism underlying post-ablation recurrence and present a promising dual-regulation strategy for remodeling the post-ablation TME to potentiate durable anti-tumor immunity.

title: Needle-free jet injection in translation: a narrative review of the state of the art, key trends, and research gaps
abstract: Needle-free jet injectors (NFJIs) deliver drugs through high-velocity liquid microjets that penetrate skin without needles, offering potential advantages in patient acceptability, sharps waste reduction, and intradermal targeting. We reviewed recent translational evidence for NFJIs with emphasis on commercially accessible spring- and gas-powered systems. A PubMed search yielded 12,364 records; 351 articles were assessed for eligibility and 143 studies (2010- February 2025) were included for analysis, with figures summarizing investigation frequency and publication count. Across studies, spring-powered devices were evaluated more evenly across in vitro, ex vivo, and in vivo stages, whereas gas-powered systems were more frequently studied in clinical trials, with comparatively limited ex vivo assessment. Commonly-investigated parameters were nozzle diameters of 150-200 μm and intradermal injection volumes of 50-100 μL. Jet performance and safety were strongly influenced by pressure/velocity, stand-off distance, formulation viscosity, and skin mechanics; velocities of ~100 m/s are frequently cited as a threshold for reliable penetration, while excessive pressure can increase splash-back and tissue trauma. Despite expanding applications e.g., vaccination, anesthesia, dermatologic intralesional therapies, translation is hindered by inconsistent reporting of jet parameters and limited standardized, quantitative endpoints. We propose that harmonized reporting and assessment methods should integrate model selection, parameter documentation, and clinically meaningful endpoints. With these key improvements reproducibility and acceleration of NFJI adoption can be achieved.

title: Uncovering the lymphatic uptake, pharmacokinetics, and biodistribution of mRNA-lipid nanoparticles after intravenous and subcutaneous injection
abstract: Lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulations have enabled the in vivo delivery of messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) vaccines and therapeutics yet the delivery of RNA remains relatively inefficient. In order to improve LNP design there is a need to better understand how current mRNA-LNP formulations are trafficked and expressed in vivo. Importantly, no prior work has quantified mRNA-LNP transport through lymphatics. In the current study we profile the thoracic lymph uptake, plasma pharmacokinetics (PK), and tissue protein expression after intravenous (IV) and subcutaneous (SC) administration in rats of three common LNP formulations (ALC-0315, SM-102 and MC3 ionizable lipids) containing muGFP-P2A-nLuc reporter mRNA. After IV administration, the SM-102 and MC3 LNP formulations provided the most effective protection of mRNA in plasma. Despite this, tissue NanoLuc® Luciferase (nLuc) expression at 32 h post-dosing was relatively similar across formulations with highest expression seen in the liver and spleen. After SC injection, all formulations supported relatively low bioavailability of mRNA (0.42-0.87% dose) and slightly higher bioavailability of ionizable and PEG lipid (<5% dose) with PK profiles of the ionizable lipid and PEG lipid not completely matching the mRNA PK profiles. There was also greater lymphatic recovery of all ionizable lipids (3.1-4.3% dose) compared to mRNA (0.62-1.4% dose) and PEG lipid (1.9-2.0% dose). Together these data suggest that mRNA is lost prior to or during lymphatic transport. Importantly, concentrations of all mRNA-LNP components were 10-1000 fold higher in thoracic lymph compared to plasma after SC injection. At 32 h after SC injection, highest nLuc expression was seen in lymph nodes and tissues near the dosing site and in the liver and spleen. These findings demonstrating that mRNA-LNPs predominantly traffic from tissue injection sites via lymphatics, mRNA-LNP components may traffic separately from each other in both lymph and blood, and tissue protein expression reflects the PK of mRNA-LNPs at early timepoints.

title: Ritlecitinib lipid microsphere development and model-facilitated determination of regional gastrointestinal delivery in healthy volunteers
abstract: Colonic drug delivery has the potential to provide therapeutic benefit for diseases like Ulcerative Colitis (UC) and Crohn's disease (CD) by elevating local drug concentrations while minimizing adverse effects associated with systemic exposure. Achieving colonic drug delivery requires deliberate formulation development optimally supported by Physiologically Based Biopharmaceutics Models (PBBMs) that may predict colonocyte exposure and drug concentration in the colonic lumen. In this study, ritlecitinib, a covalent inhibitor of JAK3 and TEC family kinases, was incorporated into modified release (MR) lipid microsphere formulations to achieve colonic delivery. To assess in vivo performance, two ritlecitinib MR formulations were administered to healthy human volunteers, pre- and post-prandially, and a ritlecitinib oral solution was administered as a control. Using a combination of the resulting pharmacokinetic dataset, ritlecitinib physicochemical properties, in vitro release profiles of the administered formulations, and formulation-specific gastrointestinal transit profiles, a PBBM was established to predict the ritlecitinib dose fraction absorbed in each gastrointestinal compartment, pre- and post-prandially. In the fasted state, the ritlecitinib dose fraction absorbed in the colon (Fa colon ) was enhanced for both the faster-releasing (Fa colon : 0.38 ± 0.07) and slower-releasing (Fa colon : 0.40 ± 0.08) MR formulations relative to the oral solution (Fa colon : 0.01 ± 0.01). In the fed state, Fa colon was consistent for the slower-releasing formulation (Fa colon : 0.38 ± 0.07), whereas Fa colon for the faster-releasing formulation was notably reduced (Fa colon : 0.27 ± 0.09), indicating that consistent colonic delivery across prandial states depends on release rate optimization. Clinical Trial Records: ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT06172348; EU CTR number 2023-505603-23-00.

title: Nanoarchitectonics via emulsion interfacial in situ polymerization for enhanced cross-presentation and antitumor immunity
abstract: Emulsion adjuvants enhance vaccine responses by forming antigen reservoirs and maintaining local immune stimulation, but their dynamic oil-water interfaces have limitations in regulating intracellular transport and cross-presentation. Here, we developed a mild in situ emulsion interface polymerization (EIIP) strategy, utilizing the oil-water interface as a confined reaction zone to generate functional polymer shells around the antigen-containing droplets. By constructing particles with consistent components, the same antigen is confined to the aqueous core or on the shell surface respectively, thereby evaluating the contribution of antigen location to immunity. Internal compartmentalization enhanced dendritic-cell maturation and MHC-I cross presentation. It retained antigen within the pH-responsive shell during intracellular trafficking, which triggered mitochondrial perturbation, cytosolic mitochondrial DNA accumulation and increased 2'3'-cGAMP. In vivo, internal antigen compartmentalization strengthened antigen-specific CD8 + T cell responses and antitumour efficacy. EIIP retains the squalene emulsion, which prolonged antigen retention at the injection site and promoted delivery to draining lymph nodes. The distinct contributions of squalene in prophylactic and therapeutic tumor models further indicate that prolonged antigen exposure and antigen localization are non-equivalent determinants of vaccine activity. EIIP turns the emulsion interface into a reaction zone, thereby alters its cross-presentation and antigen-specific CD8 + T cell response.

title: Tetrahedral DNA engineered Janus nanoplatform for potentiated Zn2+ interference therapy and cGAS-STING activation via efficient delivery of exogenous DNA
abstract: While zinc-ion interference therapy presents a compelling approach for cancer immunotherapy, poor intracellular bioavailability and weak innate immune activation restrict its therapeutic potential. To overcome these bottlenecks, we developed tetrahedral DNA-integrated ZnFe 2 O 4 -ZnO Janus nanoparticles (TDN-ZIZJP) to achieve spatiotemporal modulation of immunity. Distinct from conventional cubic nanoparticles, this nail-shaped Janus architecture amplifies cell-particle interactions, substantially improving tumor penetration and cellular uptake. This unique feature endows improved selectively dissolving of ZnO domain within the mildly acidic tumor microenvironment, resulting in a targeted intracellular surge of Zn 2+ . This enhanced ion flux provokes oxidative stress and endogenous DNA damage, thereby increasing the availability of endogenous cytosolic DNA. Moreover, the integrated tetrahedral DNA nanostructures serve as a robust reservoir, delivering abundant exogenous dsDNA directly into the cytoplasm. Zn 2+ -induced endogenous DNA release and TDN-derived exogenous dsDNA jointly increase the availability of cytosolic DNA substrates for cGAS. This dual-source DNA supply supports sustained cGAS-STING activation, thereby enhancing type I interferon signaling, promoting dendritic cell maturation and increasing cytotoxic T-cell infiltration. This study provides a new avenue that couples Zn 2+ -mediated ion interference and endogenous DNA damage with an exogenous dsDNA reservoir, providing a highly tunable platform for metal ion-regulated immunotherapy.

A modular nucleic acid-albumin biomolecular platform for multifunctional drug designs
abstract: The nanomedicine field has seen a paradigm shift towards multifunctional drug designs to maximise drug efficacy. Assembly of functionalised oligonucleotide (ODN) modules onto an albumin scaffold is an attractive solution offering a technological advancement in albumin-based drug delivery we apply in this work for a T-Cell Engager (TCE) and Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor (ICI) immuno-oncology combination. The "plug-and-play" modular approach was used to incorporate an anti-programmed cell death protein ligand 1 (anti-PD-L1) nanobody-ODN module onto a bispecific anti-EGFR x anti-CD3 scFv-albumin TCE fusion. Cys34 ODN site-specific conjugation on albumin allowed subsequent base-driven annealing of the complementary anti-PD-L1 nanobody-ODN module offering an easy and versatile alternative to established protein engineering approaches. The biomolecular components elements demonstrated effective binding of cellular targets in vitro, efficient PD-1/PD-L1 axis blockade and enhanced T-cell mediated cancer cell killing compared to single or separate combined treatments. Modular assembly on an albumin scaffold engineered with high neonatal Fc receptor affinity increased the circulatory half-life in humanised FcRn/albumin mice from 18.8 h to 26.6 h compared to wild type albumin sequences. This biomolecular assembly reflects the transition in the field towards multifunctional platforms exemplified in this work with an ICI and TCE combination promoting application for a range of functionalities and drug class combinations and offering programable half-life through inclusion of albumin sequences with different FcRn affinities.

title: Advancing extracellular vesicle therapeutics by chemical biology
abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) possess favorable biocompatibility and diverse biological functions, making them promising platforms for therapeutic delivery. However, realizing their full delivery potential requires precise engineering of EVs with tailored functionalities. By bridging chemical tools and biological systems, chemical biology provides a versatile toolkit for the modular engineering of EVs. Here, we provide a systematic overview of recent progress in chemical biology-enabled EV engineering, with an emphasis on three main strategies including protein engineering, nucleic acid engineering, and glycoengineering. In this review, we discuss the design principles of representative approaches and assess their practical utility and performance. Particular attention is given to the integration of orthogonal engineering strategies to coordinate multiple delivery functions within a single EV platform. We further discuss emerging opportunities in multi-specific vesicular antibody design and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted engineering. By linking molecular engineering strategies with specific delivery requirements, this review provides a comprehensive chemical biology-based framework for the rational design of engineered EVs with tailored delivery functions.

title: In vivo chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy: From mechanistic innovation to clinical translation
abstract: Conventional ex vivo chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy is limited by cumbersome manufacturing workflows, prohibitive costs and various treatment-related risks. In vivo CAR-T technology directly generates engineered cells within patients, conferring distinct advantages in operational simplicity, biosafety and clinical accessibility. This review systematically evaluates existing delivery platforms and classifies in vivo CAR-T into two core paradigms: persistent engineering and transient reprogramming, each featuring distinct properties tailored to different clinical indications. It further summarizes preclinical advances and clinical data covering hematological malignancies, solid tumors, autoimmune disorders and organ fibrosis, in which numerous investigational candidates have exhibited encouraging efficacy. Ultimately, five translational barriers summarized as the 5S challenges (specificity, stability, safety, suppression and scalability) and their matched optimization tactics are comprehensively discussed. This review provides a clinician-oriented decision matrix that links carriers selection to disease biology, and a 5S optimization framework to guide next-generation vector design. Collectively, these insights establish a translational roadmap for customizing in vivo CAR-T design to specific clinical indications and take a critical step toward realizing the full therapeutic potential of this disruptive modality.

title: Overcoming technological and biological barriers to pulmonary mRNA delivery with lipid-polymer hybrid nanoparticles
abstract: Delivering mRNA to the lungs promises treatment of genetic, infectious and non-communicable lung diseases. Yet, conventional lipid nanoparticle formulations lack the stability needed to endure the harsh mechanical stress during nebulization. Additionally, once deposited in the respiratory tract, gene delivery systems may first have to overcome the mucus barrier, before actually transfecting the target cells. To overcome these challenges, we utilize lipid-polymer hybrid nanoparticles (LPH), merging the stability of pharmaceutical polymers with the transfection efficiency of cationic and ionizable lipids. LPH are produced in a robust microfluidic process, accomplish near-complete encapsulation efficiency, even after nebulization, and confer high transfection efficiency in A549 cells. To provide colloidal stability after aerosolization, we developed a coating strategy with hyaluronic acid (HA) and poly(vinyl alcohol) (PVA), ensuring ideal nebulization stability by steric shielding. This formulation showed good transfection efficiency of air-liquid interface grown Calu-3 cells, producing and covered by mucus. The potential of LPH to deliver mRNA to mammalian cells was first shown in primary human lung fibroblasts in vitro and could also be confirmed after intratracheal administration to mice in vivo. Together, these findings validate LPH as a versatile and aerosolizable mRNA delivery platform, overcoming the key technological and biological barriers in pulmonary gene delivery.

title: mRNA folding facilitates efficient and spleen-targeted delivery by highly branched poly(β-amino ester)s
abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA)-based therapeutics hold great promise in preventing and treating various diseases. However, the instability and high immunogenicity of raw mRNA molecules, along with the inefficient delivery vectors, strictly limited the proteins translation and therapeutic applications. In this work, we successfully engineered a folded structural mRNA for enhancing its stability by leveraging a magnesium ion (Mg 2+ )-mediated charge neutralization and structural compression strategy. Further, a functionalized highly branched poly(β-amino ester)s (HPAEs) was utilized to efficiently deliver the folded mRNA, achieving specifically targeting to the spleen. Notably, compared with polyplexes containing non-folded mRNA, the optimal folded mRNA-based polyplexes exhibited stronger mRNA encapsulation, smaller size, and a more homogeneous morphology; ultimately, demonstrated higher mRNA transfection efficiency up to 85.4% across five different cell types, maintaining high cell viability. Mechanistic studies demonstrated that Mg 2+ -mediated mRNA folding strategy dramatically enhanced the folded mRNA-formulated polyplexes cellular uptake and endosomal escape. Encouragingly, when administered systemically, the representative folded mRNA-based polyplexes demonstrated robust protein expression, yielding 3-fold enhancement in spleen, compared to the unfolded mRNA-based nanoparticles, showing superior biosafety in vivo. Collectively, the work establishes a new class of the folded structure mRNA polymer delivery system, and provides a foundation for the next generation of RNA-based therapeutic drugs for spleen-related diseases.

A zinc-sequestering polymer disrupts zinc homeostasis to suppress fungal viability and virulence
abstract: Zinc is a central structural cofactor in fungi, supporting transcriptional control and mitochondrial function, and its tightly regulated homeostasis presents an underexploited antifungal intervention point. Targeting zinc-dependent architectures offers a mechanistically distinct alternative to conventional membrane- or cell wall-directed antifungals. Here we report a zinc- deprivation fungicide (ZDF) by grafting high-affinity bipyridine chelators onto ε-poly-l-lysine, enabling intracellular sequestration of labile zinc without overt membrane disruption. ZDF-induced zinc depletion disrupts zinc-dependent RNA processing, particularly mitochondrial tRNA modification, thereby collapsing mitochondrial translation, impairing oxidative phosphorylation, and inducing profound energetic failure. ZDF further remodels zinc-dependent regulatory networks, downregulating drug efflux to restore azole-resistant strains and suppressing biofilm maturation via zinc-responsive Zap1-Dpp1-farnesol axis. This strategy shows high selectivity over mammalian cells, and outperforms clinical azoles in murine cutaneous wound and rabbit keratitis models. By employing the unique role of zinc as an essential structural cofactor for fungal transcriptional regulators, this work defines intracellular zinc sequestration as a non-membrane-directed antifungal strategy that exploits a central regulatory dependency in fungi.

title: Self-augmenting procoagulant microspheres potentiate microvessel embolization and hypoxia-activated prodrug activation against hepatocellular carcinoma
abstract: Transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) persists a cornerstone therapy for hypervascular tumors such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), yet clinical limitations remain due to inefficient occlusion of tumor microvessels and hypoxia-induced drug resistance. Here, self-augmenting procoagulant microspheres (SPM) were developed for sustained co-delivery of thrombin (Th) and hypoxia-activated prodrug AQ4N (Th/AQ@SPM) to potentiate TACE therapy in HCC. SPM induced primary embolization by obstructing major tumor vasculature, affording vascular disruption and procoagulant factor exposure to establish a localized hypercoagulable microenvironment. Th-triggered secondary thrombosis through platelet aggregation and fibrinogen-to-fibrin conversion within residual vasculature extended occlusion to inter-microsphere spaces and distal microvessels beyond direct microsphere reach. Concurrently, hypoxia-potentiated activation of AQ4N to its cytotoxic form enabled targeted chemotherapy within the ischemic tumors. In rabbit renal and auricular artery models, Th@SPM demonstrated significant microvessel embolization through dual-phase vascular occlusion. Orthotopic VX2 liver tumor models revealed that TACE treatment with Th/AQ@SPM achieved superior tumor suppression without adverse toxic effects. Thus, Th/AQ@SPM establishes a self-augmenting embolic cascade that couples progressive microvascular occlusion with hypoxia-activated chemotherapy, providing a potent strategy to overcome key limitations of conventional TACE for HCC.

title: Lysosome-resident nanoreactor enables spatiotemporally controlled ferroptosis via cascade amplification of lipid peroxidation in breast cancer therapy
abstract: Ferroptosis induced by Fenton-reaction holds great promise in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) therapy. However, its efficacy is severely constrained by limited endogenous hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) substrates and poor Fenton reaction efficiency. To overcome these limitations, we propose a strategy to initiate a heterogeneous photo-Fenton-like reaction in H 2 O 2 -rich lysosomes and design a reaction engine for amplified cascade toxic oxidative radical propagation (REACTOR), which can confine the reaction to lysosomes for light triggering and accelerate it with p-benzoquinone (DMBQ). The REACTOR nanoplatform encapsulates copper-enriched Prussian blue (CuPB) and a redox-active DMBQ within thermosensitive liposomes, enabling preferential accumulation in lysosomes. Under irradiation, REACTOR triggers lipid phase transition, exposing the co-encapsulated CuPB and DMBQ to the lysosomal H 2 O 2 pool and initiating a highly efficient Fenton reaction that induces lysosomal membrane lipid peroxidation. Concurrently, ferrous ions released from lysosomal stores, together with CuPB-catalyzed quinone redox cycle, propagate oxidative damage to mitochondrial membranes, culminating in an explosive burst of lipid peroxides that efficiently triggers ferroptosis. REACTOR combined with irradiation significantly inhibits tumor growth, even achieving complete tumor regression and effectively suppressing metastasis in a TNBC-model. This light-activatable REACTOR transitions from a ready to a reactive state by mimicking the bombardier beetle's defense strategy, leveraging the lysosomal compartment to trigger, amplify, and sustain oxidative damage, offering a highly efficient and low-toxicity platform for precision cancer therapy.

title: Validation of senescence as a therapeutic target in metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH) through navitoclax delivery
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) is a chronic liver disease characterized by steatosis, inflammation, and progressive fibrosis. Increasing evidence suggests that cellular senescence contributes to MASH progression by promoting lipid accumulation, inflammatory signaling, and fibrogenic responses, highlighting hepatic senescent cells as a potential therapeutic target. Senolytics selectively eliminate senescent cells, but their application in MASH remains insufficiently explored. In this study, we developed in vitro models integrating hepatic lipid accumulation and hepatocyte-macrophage inflammatory crosstalk to facilitate investigation of the contribution of cellular senescence to MASH pathology and to evaluate senescence-targeted interventions. Senescent hepatic cells showed enhanced lipid accumulation and amplified inflammatory signaling with macrophages. Natural Extracellular Vesicles (EVs) derived from adipocytes reduced senescence-associated phenotypes but exhibited context-dependent biological effects, highlighting the limited control over their intrinsic bioactivity. Navitoclax, a senolytic targeting anti-apoptotic BCL-2 family proteins, reduced senescence-associated phenotypes, but its clinical use is limited by its dose-dependent toxicity. Hence, we conceived nano-Cell Vesicle Technology Systems (nCVTs), a biohybrid-based platform combining cell-derived membranes with synthetic lipids for controlled delivery of navitoclax. Navitoclax-loaded nCVTs retained senolytic activity and reduced inflammatory signaling and fibrotic activation in vitro. Importantly, in a Western diet- and fructose-induced (WDF) MASH mouse model, navitoclax-loaded AML-12-derived nCVTs alleviated hepatic lipid accumulation while reducing histopathological activity score and fibrotic profiles. Neither navitoclax formulation reduced platelet counts or hemoglobin concentrations at the tested dose. Collectively, these findings support cellular senescence as a therapeutically relevant target for MASH and identify nCVTs as a promising engineered platform for controlled senolytic delivery.

Translational resilience in intravaginal HIV prevention and multipurpose prevention technologies: formulation, exposure, and implementation barriers
abstract: Intravaginal HIV prevention has progressed from early nonspecific microbicides to antiretroviral gels, films, inserts, and intravaginal rings, alongside emerging biologic agents and multipurpose prevention technologies (MPTs). Despite substantial advances in antiviral potency and formulation technology, translation from pharmaceutical development to consistent clinical protection has remained uneven, indicating that API activity or dosage-form performance alone is insufficient to explain clinical outcomes. This review critically examines the development of intravaginal HIV prevention and MPT products through a mechanistic pharmaceutical perspective, focusing on the relationships between controllable product attributes, drug release and transport, the cervicovaginal environment, compartment-specific pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics (PK/PD), and product use. Historical microbicide and antiretroviral programs are examined as translational case studies to identify how mucosal safety, local exposure and use-dependent drug delivery contributed to divergent clinical outcomes. The review further evaluates how cervicovaginal fluid, semen, mucus, epithelial barriers, hormonal state, microbiome composition, and inflammation can modify formulation behavior and drug transport; how API physicochemistry, solid state, drug loading, drug-polymer partitioning, and diffusivity constrain formulation architecture and release; and how these relationships differ among gels, films, inserts, sustained-release devices, MPTs, and biologic delivery systems. Particular attention is given to the distinction between drug incorporation, release, tissue transport, and pharmacologically relevant exposure, and to the additional challenges created when multiple APIs require different release rates, biological compartments, or durations of action. Platform characteristics are further considered in relation to the exposure patterns and product-use conditions they are intended to support. By integrating formulation science with cervicovaginal physiology, PK/PD, and clinical experience, this review provides a mechanistic basis for identifying where intravaginal prevention systems lose translational performance and which formulation-transport-exposure relationships require stronger evidence to support more reproducible clinical protection.
